note: Hypothetical values, supplied to practise experimental design. The score below is an invented composite, not a physical measurement, and it was not produced by a real encoder. Conclusions drawn here are about experimental reasoning, not about codec behaviour.
source: audio/source -- the same thirty-second recording as week 2

measure.name: Simplified deviation score
measure.unitNote: The score is built from per-band differences expressed in decibels, but adding eight of them together does not produce a decibel quantity. It is an arbitrary composite on its own scale, useful only for comparing conditions inside this scenario.
measure.howTo: For each of the eight frequency bands, take the absolute difference in band energy between the condition and the source, in dB. Add the eight numbers. The result is one score per condition.
measure.repeatabilityNote: Repeating the whole procedure and recomputing the difference between two conditions moves that difference by up to 0.5 score points. The figure is the repeatability of a pairwise difference, not of a single score, because a comparison is what you are reporting. A difference of 0.5 or less is a non-detection: this scenario gives you no basis for saying the conditions differ.

conditions.label: Exact digital copy
conditions.note: Copied byte for byte ten times. No encoder involved.

comparisons.label: The comparison you are given
comparisons.claim: Ten encoding cycles cause a large loss.

comparisons.label: Corrected, at 128 kbps
comparisons.claim: At 128 kbps, ten cycles produce a difference detectable in this scenario.

comparisons.label: Corrected, at 320 kbps
comparisons.claim: At 320 kbps, ten cycles produce no difference this procedure can detect.

reveal.confound: Comparison M changes two things at once: the number of encoding cycles (1 to 10) and the bitrate (320 to 96). Its 9.5-point difference cannot be attributed to either variable.
reveal.corrected: Holding the bitrate fixed isolates the cycle count. At 128 kbps the difference is 3.2 points, which is detectable in this scenario. At 320 kbps it is 0.4 points, at or below the 0.5-point repeatability, which is a non-detection.
reveal.conclusion: Inside this scenario the effect of re-encoding depends on the bitrate. At 320 kbps, ten cycles produced no detectable difference. A non-detection is a finding with a specific meaning -- any effect is smaller than this procedure can resolve -- and it is not the same as no effect existing. The confounded comparison gave a difference roughly three times larger than the isolated one at the bitrate where a difference was detectable.
reveal.limits: One source, one invented score, one hypothetical setup. The score sums eight bands and would miss a change confined to a narrower range, or one that does not appear as band energy at all. Nothing here licenses a claim about how any real codec behaves, at any bitrate.
